title: Introduce cost-control-flow: tenant policy engine for batching & cache defaults
author: Priya Nambiar
description:
Motivation: Customers want predictable unit economics without manually tuning batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles for every tenant and workload. This PR introduces the "cost-control-flow" subsystem: a small, opinionated policy engine that synthesizes tenant-level defaults for batching, prefix cache, and quantization fallbacks with safe fallthroughs and a simulation mode.

High level changes:
- Add a lightweight policy engine (pkg/policy/cost_control.go, pkg/policy/engine_test.go) that evaluates tenant policies written as ordered rules. Rules are intentionally limited (match by route, traffic class, and latency bucket) to keep evaluation O(#rules) and auditable.
- Expose tenant config keys under: tenant.config.cost_control.{enabled,policy_id,cache_ttl_secs,batch_target_ms,quant_fallback_priority}. These are stored as JSON blobs in the existing tenant store (no schema migration required).
- Implement server-side defaults synthesizer (cmd/rcost/synthesizer.go) that produces conservative defaults per tenant using recent traffic histograms (20k samples) and a cost budget target. Defaults are designed to never increase tail latency by >3% compared to a baseline.
- CLI: rcost simulate --tenant T123 --policy p-default --workload-file samples/web-chat.json produces a short report (expected unit cost delta, estimated p95 change) so SREs/product teams can iterate offline.
- Runtime integration: the serving runtime now reads an evaluated policy response in routing-time metadata and applies three no-op-safe knobs: target batching window (ms), cache TTL hint (secs), and quantization preference order. The runtime will not apply the policy if doing so would violate a hard SLA (configured per route).
- Observability: added metrics (policy_eval.duration_ms, policy_eval.hit_count, cost_control.applied_count) and two logs for audit (policy_eval.request_id -> rule_id, synthesized_defaults.snapshot_id).
- Safety & rollback: feature gated behind tenant flag and deploy flag. If any CI smoke test fails, rollout is blocked. There is an automatic revert to conservative defaults if policy evaluation error rate > 0.5% over 5m.

Design notes and rationale:
- Keep policy language intentionally small so we can ship quickly and retain strong performance characteristics. This is not a general-purpose policy DSL, it's a cost-control flow aimed at safe defaults and tenant isolation.
- Use post-hoc synthesis (rcost synth) rather than direct learning in the control plane to avoid feedback loops that could destabilize latency.

Behavioral guarantees:
- No policy will be applied if (1) it increases route p95 by >5ms absolute, or (2) the tenant has an SLA tag requiring strict latency.
- Quantization fallbacks are only advisory; runtime refuses to switch to a quant profile that hasn't been validated in the model registry for the target hardware.

Checklist:
- [x] Policy engine implementation + unit tests
- [x] Synthesizer CLI + sample workload and simulation test harness
- [x] Runtime hook integration and guardrail checks
- [x] Observability metrics + sample Grafana dashboard JSON (docs/grafana/cost-control-dashboard.json)
- [x] Docs: docs/operations/cost-control-flow.md with onboarding steps and example policy templates
- [x] E2E smoke: synthetic web-chat workload validated on dev cluster (latency regression within targets)

Migration/rollout plan:
1) Deploy code behind feature flag to canary region; enable only for internal tenants.
2) Run rcost simulate across top-5 tenant workloads to generate candidate policies.
3) Enable per-tenant opt-in with a 2-week monitoring window; if any significant regressions detected revert per-tenant flags.
4) Expand to self-serve tenants after two weeks of stable metrics.

Related work: ENG-2382 (policy engine prototype), ENG-2419 (tenant telemetry sampler).

Notes for reviewers: The synthesizer contains a small heuristic budget allocator; I'm particularly interested in feedback on the cost-to-latency model (pkg/rcost/model_estimator.go). I kept the model intentionally conservative (bias toward not increasing latency).

review_comments: Evan Park: Can you explain why we opted for ordered rules vs. a priority hash? Looks good but I'd like clarity on complexity guarantees.
Priya Nambiar: Ordered rules keep semantics simple and auditable; evaluation is O(n) and n is expected to be <50 per tenant. Added comment in engine.go to justify choice.
Marisol Ortega: The cost-to-latency estimator seems optimistic for long-tail workloads. Can we bias it more conservatively?
Priya Nambiar: Updated estimator to add a 2% latency safety margin and added an integration test with a heavy-tail synthetic trace. See model_estimator.go change.
Jonah Liu: CI flaked on the gRPC auth test in the canary run. Rerunning...
Priya Nambiar: Flake was unrelated; rebase fixed the transient failure. CI is green now.
release_notes: Introduce a tenant-level cost-control flow and policy engine that generates safe batching/cache/quantization defaults. Includes a simulator CLI (rcost simulate) and observability hooks. Rollout is opt-in and gated by feature flags.
